to avoid aggravation of fecal incontinence (FI) symptoms associated with recurrent OASIS by subsequent vaginal delivery and to avoid unnecessary cesarean section. In such cases, it is necessary to consider FI symptoms, endoanal ultrasonography findings, and anal manometry as well as obstetric conditions and the wishes of the pregnant woman. In women with a history of OASIS, its recurrence rate at the subsequent vaginal delivery has been reported to be 4.4%-9.0%[ - ]. Edozien et al.[ ] investigated the course of 639,402 primiparas using the UK health insurance medical database and found that 24.2% of the women with a history of OASIS at the first vaginal delivery delivered by cesarean section at the second delivery, whereas only 1.5% of the women without a history of OASIS delivered by cesarean section at the second delivery. In addition, the incidence of OASIS in women who delivered by vaginal delivery at the second delivery was 5.5 times significantly higher among pregnant women with a history of OASIS (7.2%) than that among pregnant women without a history of OASIS (1.3%). Jango et al.[ ] studied 1,490 women with a history of OASIS at their first vaginal delivery who delivered by vaginal delivery at their second delivery and found that OASIS recurred at the second delivery in 106 (7.1%) of them. In addition, the proportion of women with FI ≥5 years after the second delivery was significantly higher in those with recurrent OASIS (25 women, 23.6%) than in those without recurrent OASIS (182 women, 13.2%). However, a systematic review (14 papers, 977 patients)[ ] examining the effect of mode of next delivery in women with a history of OASIS showed no significant association between mode of subsequent delivery and anal incontinence. Therefore, anal incontinence may develop or aggravate when pregnant women with a history of OASIS give birth by vaginal delivery, but it is inconclusive whether the prevalence of anal incontinence will increase significantly. Scheer et al.[ ] prospectively evaluated 59 pregnant women with a history of OASIS by adopting a protocol in which cesarean section was performed in cases where endoanal ultrasonography showed an anal sphincter defect ≥30° and a voluntary contraction pressure increase of <20 mmHg, whereas vaginal delivery was performed in all other cases. As a result, 47 women were assigned to vaginal delivery and 12 to cesarean section; however, 3 women in the cesarean section group preferred vaginal delivery, five women in the vaginal delivery group preferred cesarean section, and 4 women had emergency cesarean section. Finally, 41 women underwent vaginal delivery, whereas 18 underwent cesarean section. Evaluation at 13 weeks after delivery showed that OASIS recurred in three women (7.3%) in the vaginal delivery group, but overall, there was no significant change in FI symptoms, QOL, and anal pressure. The guideline published by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists[ ], also adopting the protocol of Scheer et al., recommends performing endoanal ultrasonography and anal manometry if FI symptoms persist in pregnant women with a history of OASIS and then considering a planned cesarean section if the abnormalities described in the protocol of Scheer et al. are observed. In contrast, if a pregnant woman has a history of OASIS but no symptoms of FI and no abnormalities described in the protocol of Scheer et al. are detected by endoanal ultrasonography and anal manometry, a vaginal delivery is recommended. Several studies have validated this protocol[ - ]. Karmarkar et al.[ ] proposed vaginal delivery in 26 cases and planned cesarean section in 24 cases based on the guideline published by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists for 50 pregnant women with a history of OASIS. Evaluation at 8-12 weeks after the subsequent delivery revealed that none of the women who had undergone vaginal delivery as planned complained of FI after delivery. Jordan et al.[ ] also proposed the mode of delivery for 122 pregnant women with a history of OASIS based on the guideline published by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, evaluated the symptoms of FI using the St. Mark's Score, and performed endoanal ultrasonography and anal manometry before and 3 months after the subsequent delivery. As a result, in 99 women who had undergone vaginal delivery, the symptoms of FI did not aggravate, and ultrasonography did not reveal any aggravation of anal sphincter injury. However, voluntary contraction pressure significantly decreased from an average of 92 mmHg to 50 mmHg. Jordan et al.[ ] also presented an algorithm in which they listed three options for women with a history of OASIS who have persistent FI symptoms and whose endoanal ultrasonography and anal manometry findings reveal obvious abnormalities. As the first option, cesarean delivery is recommended if the FI symptoms are mild. As the second option, if the FI symptoms are severe, vaginal delivery is recommended if the patient

However, voluntary contraction pressure significantly decreased from an average of 92 mmHg to 50 mmHg. As the first option, cesarean delivery is recommended if the FI symptoms are mild. As the second option, if the FI symptoms are severe, vaginal delivery is recommended if the patient wishes to give birth to a second child, based on the expectation that it is unlikely for FI symptoms to further aggravate. As the third option, anal sphincteroplasty is recommended if the patient does not wish to give birth to any more children. In addition, the Incontinence 6 th Edition[ ] also adopted the algorithm of Jordan et al. However, for the second option, the patient will experience severe FI in the subsequent pregnancy and delivery, but this could be avoided by undergoing anal sphincteroplasty before the next pregnancy to improve FI and reconsidering and selecting the mode of delivery based on FI symptoms and examination results. In contrast, Abramowitz et al.[ ] conducted an RCT in which 222 pregnant women who had grade 3 OASIS but without FI were randomly assigned to the vaginal delivery group (112 women) and the cesarean section group (110 women). Evaluation after 6 months from the delivery revealed that aggravation of anal sphincter injury as shown by ultrasonography occurred in significantly more women in the vaginal delivery group (22.4%) than in the cesarean section group (only 2.2%). However, the median St. Mark's Score was one point for both groups, indicating no significant difference. Therefore, it was concluded that cesarean section should not be uniformly recommended to patients with a history of OASIS but no symptoms of FI. In addition, in clinical studies on modes of subsequent delivery for pregnant women with a history of OASIS, endoanal ultrasonography and anal manometry are often performed. However, it is currently not possible to perform both tests on all eligible pregnant women in Japan because only a limited number of facilities can perform both tests. Therefore, when it is not possible to perform both tests, the pregnant women and their physicians should thoroughly discuss the mode of their subsequent delivery, considering the presence or absence and severity of FI symptoms as well as obstetric conditions and the wishes of the pregnant woman. 2. Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) Statement • Sacral neuromodulation is recommended for patients in whom conservative therapies are ineffective or not feasible. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 90.9%), Level of Evidence: A Abstract Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is a treatment designed to improve various pelvic floor dysfunctions, including defecation disorders, such as fecal incontinence (FI) and constipation; lower urinary tract dysfunction, such as urinary incontinence and difficulty urinating; and pelvic floor dysfunction, including chronic pelvic pain, by electrically stimulating the sacral nerve. SNM involves two stages: the first surgical procedure places a stimulation lead, allowing for evaluation of efficacy over a test stimulation period of approximately 2 weeks. In cases where the test is effective, a second procedure implants a nerve stimulator, while the stimulation lead is removed if the test is ineffective. A key feature of SNM is its ability to select effective cases through this test stimulation and its reversibility, which allows patients to return to their original state without worsening symptoms if the treatment is not effective. SNM has demonstrated excellent short- and long-term outcomes for FI and is indicated for all patients in whom conservative therapies have failed and test stimulation is safe to perform. Its adverse events include pain and infection at the implantation site. Some examinations and treatments are contraindicated for concomitant use with SNM; thus, surgeons performing SNM are required to attend a seminar. Commentary In Japan, this surgical treatment has been covered by insurance for FI since April 2014 and for refractory overactive bladder since September 2017, with insurance points allocated to each of the two surgical procedures: stimulation lead placement and stimulator implantation. Although a relatively new surgical treatment in Japan, it has a long history globally. The efficacy of this treatment for treating urinary incontinence was first reported in the United States in 1982, and the implantation of a stimulator for treating FI was first performed in Europe in 1995[ , ]. SNM has already been approved as a treatment device for FI in Europe and the United States, and as of April 2021, approximately 345,000 cases of pelvic floor dysfunction have been treated with SNM worldwide. The efficacy of SNM for FI has been demonstrated in favorable short-term[ , ] and long-term outcomes[ , , ].

In a US clinical trial[ ], test stimulation was performed in 133 patients, and the stimulator was implanted in 120 patients (90%). Of these, 106 patients were evaluable after 1 year, and 88 (83%) were successfully treated (with a reduction of >50% in FI; same below), and 43 (41%) achieved complete continence, with significant improvement in the FIQL Scale. A study on 76 patients in this clinical trial who had undergone implantation for >5 years revealed good long-term outcomes with a success rate of 89% and complete continence maintained in 36% of patients. A study on the long-term outcomes in 235 patients in the UK showed that favorable outcomes were maintained 9 years after surgery and 12 years after surgery when a telephone survey was conducted, with complete continence achieved in 21 (12.5%) and 12 (10.4%) patients, respectively[ ]. Furthermore, in a study of 325 patients in the Netherlands, 52.7% of the patients maintained efficacy over a mean follow-up period of 7.1 years, showing good long-term outcomes but no improvement in QOL[ ]. In the first Japanese multicenter study[ ] reported in 2014, test stimulation was performed in 22 patients, and implantation was performed in 21 patients (95%). Of these, 18 (86%) were successfully treated after 6 months and 4 (19%) achieved complete continence. In Europe, a study of 432 patients during the test stimulation phase found better outcomes in women than in men, with significantly higher implantation rates for delivery trauma and idiopathic FI compared with other causes[ ]. In France, a multicenter study of 352 patients showed similar efficacy in younger (<70 years) and older (>70 years) groups, indicating effectiveness in older populations[ ]. Regarding the cause-specific outcomes of SNM for FI, good outcomes with a success rate of 75% were reported for idiopathic FI without anal sphincter injury[ ]; however, even patients with anal sphincter injury achieved outcomes comparable to those in patients without anal sphincter injury[ ]. In addition, in a systematic review[ ] on the efficacy of SNM for LARS, a defecation disorder including FI after rectal cancer surgery, the stimulator was implanted in 34 (79%) of 43 patients who had undergone test stimulation, and symptoms improved in 32 (74%) of the patients. Furthermore, a meta-analysis on LARS showed significant improvement in both the CCFIS and LARS scores[ ], and efficacy comparable to that on other causes of FI was achieved[ ]. Moreover, the efficacy of SNM for FI following surgery for rectal prolapse[ ], Crohn's disease[ ], ulcerative colitis[ ], and cauda equina syndrome[ ] has also been reported. In other words, it is not possible to determine the indication for SNM based on the cause of FI. SNM is indicated for all patients in whom conservative therapies are ineffective and test stimulation can be safely performed. The precise mechanism of SNM is not fully understood but is considered multifactorial. By electrically stimulating the sacral nerve plexus, it induces contraction of the anal sphincter and levator ani muscles via the pudendal nerve, influences the sensory and autonomic nerves of the colorectal region via the pelvic plexus, and exerts effects on the central nervous system via the spinal cord[ ]. Approximately 40% of patients with FI have urinary incontinence, and approximately 25% of patients with urinary incontinence have FI[ ]. Because SNM is an effective treatment for both types of incontinence, patients with double incontinence can expect simultaneous improvement of both symptoms. According to a systematic review (6 papers, 113 patients)[ ], when SNM was performed on patients with double incontinence, the average improvement rate was 87% (44%-100%) for FI, 67% (20%-100%) for urinary incontinence, and 62% (20%-100%) for double incontinence. With respect to adverse events, pain at the implantation site was the most common at approximately 25%, followed by infection at the implantation site at approximately 10%[ , ]. In a US clinical trial[ ], modification, replacement, and removal of the stimulator were performed in 6%, 7%, and 11% of patients, respectively. However, most of the other adverse events could be managed with conservative treatment, program adjustments, and follow-up. CQ4. Which of the following should be applied first for fecal incontinence caused by laceration of the anal sphincter: anal sphincteroplasty or sacral neuromodulation? Statement • Because it remains unclear which treatment should be prioritized, the decision should be made on a case-by-case basis after thoroughly explaining the characteristics, advantages, disadvantages, and expected outcomes of each treatment method and obtaining informed consent from the patient. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Commentary Currently, there are no reports of RCTs of anal sphincteroplasty and SNM for laceration of the anal sphincter. Thus, the optimal first-line treatment remains a subject of debate. Therefore, the characteristics as well as advantages and disadvantages, including treatment outcomes, of each treatment method ( ) should be fully explained to the patient before selecting and agreeing on a treatment method on a case-by-case basis in consultation with the patient based on their condition, medical status, and wishes. In a study on SNM in 91 patients without laceration of the anal sphincter and 54 patients with a mean 105° laceration of the anal sphincter[ ], both groups showed significant improvement in fecal incontinence (FI) scores (CCFIS and St. Mark's Score) 12 months after surgery, indicating similar efficacy. In addition, a prospective study on SNM in 21 patients with laceration of the anal sphincter up to 120° and 32 patients without laceration[ ] also showed comparable efficacy in CCFIS and FIQL over a 12-month follow-up period. In a systematic review of SNM for patients with anal sphincter lacerations[ ], the CCFIS decreased from 16.5 to 3.8. However, nine of the studies included in the review were retrospective, excluding the aforementioned prospective study, indicating a low level of evidence. Furthermore, in a study comparing treatment outcomes in 13 women who underwent anal sphincteroplasty and 13 women who underwent SNM for FI caused by laceration of the anal sphincter, with matching patient backgrounds[ ], the CCFIS improved significantly only in the SNM group. In contrast, the long-term outcomes of anal sphincteroplasty for laceration of the anal sphincter remain at an efficacy rate of 10%-46% 5 years after surgery[ , ]. Because the evaluation method is not constant, it is difficult to simply compare the surgical outcomes of anal sphincteroplasty with those of SNM. However, the long-term outcomes (in a median period of 9 years and 3 months) of 160 patients who had undergone anal sphincteroplasty showed that the percentage of patients with a reduction of ≥50% in the frequency of FI (patients judged to have been successfully treated by SNM) was 60%, which was comparable to the long-term outcomes of SNM[ ]. In a study on the evolution of the two treatment methods at six facilities in Europe and the United States[ ], 284 cases of SNM and 177 cases of anal sphincteroplasty had been performed for laceration of the anal sphincter from 2000 to 2013. In addition, a single-year comparison showed that in 2000, 95.3% of patients underwent anal sphincteroplasty first, but in 2013, 82.6% of patients underwent SNM first, indicating a significant paradigm shift in approximately 10 years. Stoma construction Statement • Stoma construction is proposed for patients with fecal incontinence in whom other treatments are ineffective or not feasible. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B Abstract In recent years, advances in stoma appliances and environmental maintenance, such as management guidance by certified nurses in wound, ostomy, and continence nursing, have improved the QoL of ostomates, making stoma construction a surgical treatment option for fecal incontinence (FI). This procedure is generally considered to be the last resort for severe FI, but it is the simplest and most fundamental solution for FI if the patient can accept the psychological issue of body image being different from others. Commentary With the publication of the first edition of these guidelines and the explicit inclusion of stoma construction in the surgical treatment algorithm[ ], the challenges for patients and medical professionals in choosing stoma construction as a treatment for FI have been lowered. Therefore, when necessary, medical professionals should provide patients with information on stoma construction as a surgical treatment option for FI. It is important to confirm each patient's acceptance of the psychological issues related to body image due to having a stoma[ ], as these issues can significantly affect their QoL. In stoma construction for FI, the anal side of the sigmoid colon is usually closed while the anus is left intact, and an end stoma is constructed using the oral side of the sigmoid colon. However, in this case, the patient may require rectal amputation in the future due to diversion colitis of the remaining empty colon[ ]. Thus, this possibility must be fully explained to the patient before stoma construction. When constructing a stoma, it is the surgeon's responsibility to employ techniques that ensure the stoma is well-formed, of adequate height, and positioned appropriately. This reduces the risk of stoma-related complications, facilitates easier stoma care, and enhances the patient's QoL[ ]. Advances in ostomy appliances and progress in environmental maintenance, such as guidance by certified nurses in wound, ostomy, and continence nursing[ ], have improved the QoL of ostomates. A comparison of QoL using the SF-36 between 71 patients with FI and 39 ostomates who had undergone stoma construction because of rectal cancer, colonic diverticulosis, or FI showed that ostomates had significantly better QoL in terms of social functioning than that of patients with FI[ ]. In addition, according to a questionnaire survey of 69 ostomates who had undergone stoma construction as a treatment for severe FI[ ], QoL was better after stoma construction than before stoma construction. Several studies have compared QoL between patients who have FI after anus-preserving surgery for rectal cancer and ostomates who had undergone permanent stoma construction following rectal amputation for rectal cancer, but no reports have found significant differences in overall QoL between the two groups[ , ]. A systematic review on follow-ups of ostomates reported improvement in overall QoL over time[ ]. Patients with spinal cord injury who underwent stoma construction for FI also demonstrated an improvement in QoL[ , ]. As described above, the construction of a stoma for treating FI may improve QoL; however, it should be noted that treatment outcomes and evidence regarding QoL differ depending on the pathology of FI.

If FI does not improve adequately with initial treatment, it is important to refer the patient to a specialized medical institution for FI[ ]. If the symptoms of FI do not adequately improve with conservative therapies at a specialized medical institution, stoma construction is an option. In such cases, it is desirable to have a team of medical care in place that can provide decision-making support regarding stoma construction[ ]. However, although the construction of a stoma for treating FI can relieve the problems and concerns caused by FI, daily stoma care becomes necessary, and stoma-related complications may arise. In this regard, the “Manual of Prevention, Treatment and Care of Intestinal Stoma-Related Complications”[ ] published by the Japanese Society of Stoma and Continence Rehabilitation and the Japan Society of Coloproctology, is useful. Because stoma-related complications lead to a decline in QoL, it is necessary to prevent them from becoming severe by appropriate assessment and intervention using assessment tools, such as ABCD-Stoma Ⓡ published by the Japanese Society of Wound, Ostomy and Continence Management[ ]. When selecting stoma construction as a treatment for FI, it is important to strive to improve the QoL of the ostomate. B. Special surgical treatment 1. Antegrade continence enema (ACE) Statement • Although ACE has some morbidities, such as wound infection and postoperative stenosis, it is a useful treatment for fecal incontinence because it can be performed in a shorter time with less lavage fluid than transanal irrigation. Abstract ACE is a treatment to improve fecal incontinence (FI) that involves keeping the colon empty with antegrade lavage via an appendiceal or cecal fistula created by laparotomy, laparoscopic surgery, or endoscopic placement[ ]. In cases after appendicectomy, a surgical technique called ileal neoappendicostomy has been reported, in which the ileum is dissected at 6 cm from the distal end of the ileum. The oral end is anastomosed to the ascending colon, and the anal side of the ileum, which has a narrow diameter, is used to substitute for the appendix[ ]. Regarding transanal irrigation, ACE is indicated for severe defecation disorders, such as frequent bowel movements and severe FI, as bowel lavage is laborious and time-consuming. Compared with transanal irrigation, the advantages of ACE are that less amount of lavage fluid needs to be infused and a shorter time is required for bowel lavage. However, minimally invasive surgery is still required. Defecation does not occur through the cecal fistula; however, body image concerns remain, although these are less severe than those associated with a stoma. Commentary ACE was first reported by Malone et al. in the UK in 1990[ ] and was mainly performed for neurogenic bowel dysfunction in children[ ]. Subsequently, it has been applied for the treatment of FI and constipation in adults[ ]. Long-term outcomes regarding the assessment of defecation function, social life, and QoL showed significant improvements in FI as well as in chronic constipation and neurogenic bowel dysfunction[ ]. In a systematic review of studies on adults[ ], 78%-100% of patients continued ACE in a follow-up period of 22.5-48 months. Additionally, a retrospective study of 75 patients showed that 64 (85%) patients continued ACE during a median follow-up period of 48 months, with the Wexner Score significantly improving from 14.3 preoperatively to 3.4 postoperatively[ ]. In patients who discontinued ACE, the reasons for ACE discontinuation were abdominal pain during the procedure and prolonged FI. In a systematic review of six studies on adults and two on children regarding ileal neoappendiceal fistula, improvement in symptoms of FI and constipation was observed in all studies, and improvement in QoL was observed in five studies[ ]. The most common early postoperative complication is wound infection at 45%[ ], and other early complications, such as intestinal perforation, have also been reported[ ]. Late complications include increased incidence of postoperative stenosis[ , ], and cases have been reported in which bougie dilatation or reconstruction was performed[ ]. With ileal neoappendiceal fistulas, there is also a high incidence of stenosis, necrosis, and suture failure at the ileal-ascending colon anastomosis site[ ]. However, these complications are primarily attributed to appendiceal fistula, and the use of gastrostomy kits, though off-label, has shown promise in significantly reducing these issues. Graciloplasty Statement • Graciloplasty is a surgical treatment that should be performed in a limited number of specialized facilities because of the complexity of the surgical procedure and the need for numerous operations to master the surgical technique. Abstract In graciloplasty, the gracilis muscle is mobilized and wrapped around the anal canal, and the tendon on the distal side of the gracilis is sewn to the opposite sciatic bone to close the anal canal with moderate pressure to maintain fecal continence[ ]. This treatment is often selected for patients with severe fecal incontinence (FI) in whom other surgical treatments are ineffective, and stoma construction is the only alternative. Commentary This surgical procedure was first reported in 1952 for FI in children[ ] and was subsequently applied to the treatment of FI in adults[ ]. There are two types of surgery: adynamic graciloplasty (AG)[ ], which simply includes muscle grafting, and dynamic graciloplasty (DG)[ ], which refers to the muscle grafting with an electrical stimulator. Conventionally, to obtain good results with this treatment, DG was considered necessary to transform gracilis muscles from type II (fast-twitch) fibers prone to fatigue into type I (slow-twitch) fibers capable of sustained contraction, similar to the external anal sphincter. However, the advent of sacral neuromodulation rendered the use of electrical stimulators in DG impractical, leading to its decline in Europe and the United States. However, the effect of DG could be obtained in AG by performing transanal electrical stimulation for 6 months after the surgery[ ]. Regarding the efficacy of this treatment, a multicenter study on DG in 123 patients with FI[ ] reported that DG was efficacious in 81 patients (66%) after 18 months, and a systematic review of DG[ ] revealed that DG was effective in 42%-85% of patients. In addition, among the 31 patients who underwent DG after abdominoperineal rectal amputation for rectal cancer, defecation function could be evaluated postoperatively in 26 patients, of which 22 (71%) maintained fecal continence in a median follow-up period of 37 months[ ]. In a study reported from Japan[ ], 15 patients with severe FI underwent graciloplasty (12 cases of AG and three cases of DG), and excluding three patients in whom a stoma was constructed, 12 patients were evaluated, of which 8 (67%) maintained fecal continence of Kirwan classification grade 2 (gas incontinence only) or higher after surgery. In an observational study of 17 patients who underwent AG, 13 (76.5%) achieved fecal continence with postoperative CCFIS of ≤2[ ]. Furthermore, an evaluation of 31 patients who underwent AG 1 year after surgery revealed that the effect was maintained in 25 (81%) of the patients[ ]. With respect to complications, in a multicenter study of 123 patients[ ], complications occurred 189 times in 91 patients (74%), and surgery for complications was performed in 49 patients (40%). A systematic review of DG[ ] reported complications at an average of 1.12 times per patient with a surgery-related mortality of 2%. In addition, cases of stoma construction due to rectal perforation and rectovaginal fistula have been reported in AG[ ]. As described above, graciloplasty is one of the most complex and difficult surgeries for FI, and numerous operations are required to master the surgical technique; thus, it should only be performed in a limited number of specialized facilities. 3. Ventral rectopexy Statement • Ventral rectopexy is effective for treating passive fecal incontinence caused by rectal intussusception, rectal prolapse, or rectocele. However, consideration should be given to the potential risk of mesh-related complications. Abstract VR is a treatment aimed at improving symptoms of fecal incontinence (FI) and defecation disorder by straightening and fixing the rectum with a mesh attached to the ventral side of the lower rectum, thereby repairing rectal intussusception, rectal prolapse, and rectocele. Patients with passive FI caused by rectal intussusception or rectocele who do not respond adequately to maximal conservative therapies can be considered for this treatment.

Ventral rectopexy Statement • Ventral rectopexy is effective for treating passive fecal incontinence caused by rectal intussusception, rectal prolapse, or rectocele. However, consideration should be given to the potential risk of mesh-related complications. Abstract VR is a treatment aimed at improving symptoms of fecal incontinence (FI) and defecation disorder by straightening and fixing the rectum with a mesh attached to the ventral side of the lower rectum, thereby repairing rectal intussusception, rectal prolapse, and rectocele. Patients with passive FI caused by rectal intussusception or rectocele who do not respond adequately to maximal conservative therapies can be considered for this treatment. In addition, eligible patients should be carefully selected by further tests, such as defecography. VR has been reported to improve FI in 62.5% of patients, making it an effective treatment. However, the incidence of mesh-related complications is 1.7%, and these complications often require surgical intervention. Therefore, obtaining a thoroughly informed consent is crucial before surgery. Commentary VR involves an abdominal approach in which the peritoneum on the right side of the rectum is incised from the sacral promontory to the rectouterine (or rectovesical) fossa. The rectovaginal (or rectoprostatic) septum is dissected down to the pelvic floor, and a mesh is secured to the ventral side of the lower rectum and sacral promontory to stabilize the rectum. VR was first reported by D'Hoore et al.[ ] in 2004 as a surgery for treating rectal prolapse and is characterized by the preservation of the autonomic nerves in the dorsal rectum. It is commonly indicated for female patients with FI caused by rectal intussusception, rectal prolapse, or rectocele. Recent studies suggest that rectal intussusception may be a precursor lesion of rectal prolapse, and their pathophysiology is considered to be common[ ]. Although the mechanism by which rectal intussusception causes FI is unclear, it has been suggested that the rectoanal inhibitory reflex is induced[ ], and resting anal canal pressure is decreased[ ]. Although the mechanism by which rectocele causes FI is unclear, a possible mechanism is that stool that is not completely expelled during defecation and remains in the rectocele leaks out after defecation[ ]. Patients with FI unresponsive to maximal conservative therapies and severe rectal intussusception (grade III or IV based on the Oxford classification) identified on defecography may benefit from VR. However, the type of FI for which VR is indicated is passive FI, particularly following defecation, rather than urge FI. VR is often performed laparoscopically and uses mesh; thus, it is called laparoscopic ventral mesh rectopexy (LVMR). In Japan, short-term outcomes of LVMR in 34 patients with severe rectal intussusception and FI revealed a ≥50% reduction in incontinence frequency in 31 patients (91%) at 1 year postoperatively[ ]. In terms of the mid- to long-term outcomes of 46 patients with rectal prolapse at the same facility, their FISI scores significantly improved from 34 to 12 in the 3 months after surgery, and 10 patients had a FISI score of 7, indicating good outcomes, 5 years after surgery[ ]. In the United Kingdom, LVMR was performed in 72 patients with severe rectal intussusception (grade III in 26 patients and grade IV in 46 patients) accompanied by FI, and their FISI score significantly improved from 31 to 15 in 1 year after surgery[ ]. Postoperative complications that have been reported included dysuria in seven patients (9.7%) and exposure of the mesh to the vagina, causing infection and requiring removal, in one patient[ ]. In addition, in a report on the long-term outcomes in 848 patients in the United Kingdom[ ], 478 patients (56%) responded to a telephone questionnaire in a median postoperative follow-up period of 7 years. Of these, 104 (22%) had symptoms of FI, and evaluation of the degree of improvement in FI symptoms after LVMR using the Likert scale revealed improvement in about 2/3 of the patients, with improvement in 70 patients (67%), no change in 20 (19%), and exacerbation in 14 (14%). In contrast, postoperative new pelvic pain was reported in six patients (8%). Furthermore, sexual function improved in 11%, remained unchanged in 71%, and exacerbated in 18%. Therefore, considering the possibilities of pelvic pain and sexual dysfunction, the authors concluded that informed consent must be obtained before surgery. A comparison of robot-assisted LVMR (187 patients) and conventional laparoscopic surgery (214 patients) showed better outcomes in CCFIS and FI symptoms for robot-assisted surgery at 3 years postoperatively[ ]. Postoperative complications reported included new pelvic pain at a high incidence (31.8% in robot-assisted surgery, 11.8% in laparoscopy), dysuria (19.1% in robot-assisted surgery and 14.7% in laparoscopy), and mesh exposure to the vagina (one case in robot-assisted surgery). The outcomes of SNM are reported to be poor in patients with severe rectal intussusception[ ]. In the study, 106 patients with FI for whom SNM was indicated underwent defecography, and severe rectal

A comparison of robot-assisted LVMR (187 patients) and conventional laparoscopic surgery (214 patients) showed better outcomes in CCFIS and FI symptoms for robot-assisted surgery at 3 years postoperatively[ ]. Postoperative complications reported included new pelvic pain at a high incidence (31.8% in robot-assisted surgery, 11.8% in laparoscopy), dysuria (19.1% in robot-assisted surgery and 14.7% in laparoscopy), and mesh exposure to the vagina (one case in robot-assisted surgery). The outcomes of SNM are reported to be poor in patients with severe rectal intussusception[ ]. In the study, 106 patients with FI for whom SNM was indicated underwent defecography, and severe rectal intussusception was observed in 36 patients (34%). When the outcomes of SNM were compared between the group with severe rectal intussusception and the group without, the success rate of test stimulation was 69% in the group with severe rectal intussusception, which was significantly lower than that in the group without severe rectal intussusception at 86%. In addition, a nerve stimulator was implanted in patients with successful test stimulation, and the median FISI score after 1 year insignificantly improved from 38 to 34 in the group with severe rectal intussusception and significantly improved from 37 to 23 in the group without severe rectal intussusception, and the treatment success rate was also significantly lower in the group with severe rectal intussusception at 16% than that in the group without severe rectal intussusception at 52%. Therefore, it may be better to perform VR before SNM in patients with passive FI accompanied by severe rectal intussusception, and it may also be better to consider performing VR in patients for whom SNM is ineffective. A systematic review of 10 studies involving 1,147 patients found a 62.5% improvement in FI following VR, with a symptom recurrence rate of 7.3%. Complications included urinary tract and wound infections, with mesh-related complications occurring in 1.1% of cases. Absorbable mesh has also been used to reduce mesh-related complications, such as mesh exposure to the vaginal or rectal surface and infection. A systematic review (eight studies, 3,956 patients)[ ] comparing nonabsorbable (synthetic) and absorbable (biological) meshes in LVMR revealed an overall complication rate of 26.2%, with mesh-related complications occurring in 67 patients (1.7%) after 1.7-124 months. The incidence of mesh-related complications was 1.9% (66/3,517 patients) for nonabsorbable mesh, which was significantly higher than that for absorbable mesh at 0.2% (1/439 patients). All mesh-related complications were of Clavien-Dindo classification grade III-b, requiring surgical treatment, such as low anterior resection and stoma construction, but there were no deaths. As described above, LV may be effective for treating FI possibly caused by rectal intussusception, and an expert consensus conference[ ] also proposed that “patients with severe rectal intussusception of grade III or IV whose symptoms of FI or defecation disorder do not improve adequately with maximal conservative therapies are relatively indicated for VR.” However, postoperative pelvic pain, sexual dysfunction, and serious mesh-related complications, even at low incidence, are concerning. Therefore, the Incontinence 6 th Edition[ ], despite stating that “VR may improve FI in carefully selected patients,” rated this treatment weak in strength of recommendation at C. In addition, VR is not even included as a treatment for FI in the latest European guideline[ ] on the management of FI and the ASCRS' Clinical Practice Guidelines[ ]. Therefore, in our guidelines, VR is included as a special surgical treatment rather than a standard treatment for FI, and it is a subject for future research. C. Other surgical treatments 1. Biomaterial injection Statement • Biomaterial injection may be useful as a minimally invasive treatment for passive fecal incontinence caused by a decrease in resting anal canal pressure. Although some injection substances have been approved in Europe and the United States, they have not been approved in Japan. Abstract Biomaterial injection is a treatment to improve fecal incontinence (FI) by injecting a biocompatible material into the anal submucosa and between the external and internal anal sphincters to cause bulging, appropriately closing the anal canal. It may be useful for treating passive FI caused by decreased resting anal canal pressure resulting from poor internal anal sphincter function. Sphinkeeper™ is approved in the EU, and Solesta Ⓡ is approved in the United States as biocompatible materials for injection, and they have been reported to be effective in improving passive FI. However, they have not been approved in Japan yet. Commentary The material selected to be injected should be biocompatible, nonallergenic, easy to inject, and non-tissue transferable. Because it was reported in 1993 that injecting polytetrafluoroethylene into the anal submucosa was effective in making FI disappear in 64% of patients[ ], the use of various biocompatible materials has been reported[ ]. However, the number of cases has been small, and complications, such as anal pain and ulceration, have been reported. Gatekeeper™ and Sphinkeeper™ (THD, Correggio, Italy) are approved in

and they have been reported to be effective in improving passive FI. However, they have not been approved in Japan yet. Commentary The material selected to be injected should be biocompatible, nonallergenic, easy to inject, and non-tissue transferable. Because it was reported in 1993 that injecting polytetrafluoroethylene into the anal submucosa was effective in making FI disappear in 64% of patients[ ], the use of various biocompatible materials has been reported[ ]. However, the number of cases has been small, and complications, such as anal pain and ulceration, have been reported. Gatekeeper™ and Sphinkeeper™ (THD, Correggio, Italy) are approved in the EU, and Solesta Ⓡ (Salix, Raleigh, USA) is approved in the United States. Gatekeeper™ is a solid material made of polyacrylonitrile, which is injected under ultrasound guidance between the internal and external anal sphincters to close the anal canal. In a report of 14 patients with FI injected with Gatekeeper™[ ], the mean frequency of FI improved from 7.1 times/week to 0.4 times/week, and the mean CCFIS improved from 12.7 to 5.1 in a mean follow-up period of 33.5 months. Sphinkeeper™ is an improved version of Gatekeeper™[ ]. In an observational study of 42 patients, the CCFIS improved significantly from 12.0 to 7.6 after surgery, and 5 patients achieved complete continence[ ]. Solesta Ⓡ , which was approved in the United States in 2011, is a liquid material of dextranomer beads/stabilized sodium hyaluronate gel, which is injected in 1 mL doses in four directions under the anal mucosa, 5 mm orally from the dentate line, to close the anal canal. In a double-blind study[ ] with the sham group as control, evaluation after 6 months showed improvement of FI in 71 of 136 patients (52%) in the Solesta Ⓡ group, with a significant difference, compared with 22 of 70 patients (31%) in the sham group. A 3-year follow-up report[ ] of 136 patients who had received Solesta Ⓡ in the double-blind study showed that the percentage of patients with a reduction of ≥50% in the frequency of FI (hereinafter referred to as success rate) was 52%, 57%, and 52% 6 months, 1 year, and 3 years after surgery, respectively, indicating good long-term outcomes. Complications reported included anal pain and injection site nodule in 2.3% of patients each and rectal bleeding in 1.5% of patients, but all were minor complications, and no serious complications occurred. Regarding further long-term outcomes, the frequency of FI decreased remarkably from a mean of 21.5 times/week before surgery to 10 times/week 1 year after surgery in 16 patients who received Solesta Ⓡ . However, it returned to 26.5 times/week in 11 patients who could be followed up to 10 years after surgery[ ]. In addition, the success rate was 56% 1 year after surgery, and 27% 10 years after surgery. As shown above, its long-term outcomes are poor; however, because Solesta Ⓡ allows for additional injections, it may be possible to inject it again when FI recurs. In an observational study of 17 patients, the first dose of Solesta Ⓡ was successful in 14 patients (83.3%). When the remaining three patients were treated with an additional dose 3 months later, all patients were successfully treated. Seven patients (41%) achieved complete continence 1 year after surgery, and the frequency of FI in the remaining 10 patients improved from an average of 6.4 times/week to 2.8 times/week[ ]. Biomaterial injection appears to be effective in the treatment of mild passive FI caused by decreased resting anal canal pressure resulting from poor internal anal sphincter function. Although the success rate is not high, at approximately 50% and the long-term outcomes are poor, because Solesta Ⓡ can be administered repeatedly, it may be possible to readminister it at recurrence. No serious complications have been reported, and biomaterial injection is a simple and minimally invasive treatment that can be performed in an outpatient setting. Thus, it is hoped that this treatment will be introduced in Japan in the future. 2. Anal sphincter regenerative therapy Statement • Anal sphincter regenerative therapy can serve as a minimally invasive treatment for fecal incontinence. It has not yet been approved in Europe and the United States, where its efficacy for treating fecal incontinence has been reported, nor has it been approved in Japan. Abstract Anal sphincter regenerative therapy is aimed at improving fecal incontinence (FI) symptoms by transplanting stem cells into the anal sphincter with reduced contractile function, thereby restoring its function. Although human clinical studies have been conducted in Europe and the United States, this therapy has not yet been approved for routine medical use in Japan. Commentary Previously, stem cell transplantation experiments have been conducted using rats as the animal model of anal sphincter dysfunction[ ], and based on the results of these experiments, randomized human trials have been conducted overseas to

been reported, nor has it been approved in Japan. Abstract Anal sphincter regenerative therapy is aimed at improving fecal incontinence (FI) symptoms by transplanting stem cells into the anal sphincter with reduced contractile function, thereby restoring its function. Although human clinical studies have been conducted in Europe and the United States, this therapy has not yet been approved for routine medical use in Japan. Commentary Previously, stem cell transplantation experiments have been conducted using rats as the animal model of anal sphincter dysfunction[ ], and based on the results of these experiments, randomized human trials have been conducted overseas to investigate the efficacy of stem cell transplantation for anal sphincters with reduced contractile function. According to the latest review[ ], there had been one case report[ ], two pilot studies[ , ], one exploratory baseline study[ ], and three RCTs[ - ] involving stem cell transplantation therapy in humans. In these seven studies, stem cell transplantation therapy for improving FI was performed on 90 humans. Furthermore, an additional RCT (158 patients)[ ] was reported after the publication of the review. The cells used were autologous myoblasts in six studies and allogenic human adipose-derived stromal/stem cells[ ] as well as autologous adipose tissue-derived multipotent cells[ ], respectively, in the remaining two studies. All these cells were transplanted into the external anal sphincter, including one case report in which the cells were also transplanted into the internal anal sphincter[ ]. In the two reports involving the transplantation of adipose tissue-derived mesenchymal stem cells, no significant difference was observed in the degree of improvement in the CCFIS between the treatment and control groups[ , ]. Conversely, in the MIAS trial, a phase II study evaluating the efficacy of culturing autologous myoblasts harvested from the quadriceps muscle and then injecting and transplanting them into the external anal sphincter in 24 patients with FI, the median CCFIS after 6 months significantly decreased in both the injection and transplantation group and the placebo group. No significant difference was observed between the two groups. However, after 12 months, only the injection and transplantation group showed sustained improvement, whereas the effect disappeared in the placebo group. Consequently, the response rate after 12 months was significantly higher in the injection and transplantation group than in the placebo group (58% vs. 8%, p = 0.03)[ ]. In an exploratory baseline study, researchers evaluated the effects of culturing autologous myoblasts harvested from the pectoral muscle. Subsequently, they injected and transplanted them into the external anal sphincter of 10 female patients with FI due to anal sphincter injury during childbirth. One year after treatment, FI symptoms and QoL improved significantly. Specifically, the frequency of FI decreased from an average of 8 times per week before surgery to 0 times per week. Additionally, the CCFIS improved from 15.3 to 1.6, and the FIQL score increased from 2.8 to 4.0[ ]. Moreover, in a study evaluating the same 10 patients 5 years later, the frequency of FI was an average of 0 times/week, the CCFIS was 0.7, and the FIQL score was 4.0, indicating that the improvement effect was maintained over the long term[ ]. Furthermore, the same anal sphincter regenerative therapy was applied to 39 patients (including five men) with urge FI caused by external anal sphincter rupture and by impaired external anal sphincter function. One year after treatment, the frequency of FI had decreased by an average of 11 times/week compared with that before surgery, the CCFIS was reduced by an average of 17, and the success rate with a reduction of ≥50% in the frequency of FI was 79.5%[ ]. More recently, an RCT[ ] on this anal sphincter regenerative therapy has been reported. When the frequency of FI after 6 months was compared among a high-concentration group (75 patients), a low-concentration group (83 patients), and a placebo group (79 patients) using different concentrations of transplanted cells, the frequency of FI decreased in all three groups of the high-concentration group (reduction in frequency of FI: 4.8 times/week), the low-concentration group (4.3 times/week), and the placebo group (3.2 times/week). However, only the high-concentration group exhibited a significant decrease in FI frequency compared with the placebo group (p = 0.02). Additionally, a subgroup analysis of this therapy identified two factors that significantly improved FI: “a history of FI of ≥10 years” and “a greater amount of FI compared with minor leakage.” Currently, the optimal cell population for transplantation, the methods, and techniques for preparing the cells, and the necessary and sufficient number of cells have not yet been fully established; however, because cell injections and transplantation have been performed safely with no reports of serious complications, it is expected that this will become an important field in the treatment of FI in the future. In summary, although no meta-analyses exist regarding anal sphincter

analysis of this therapy identified two factors that significantly improved FI: “a history of FI of ≥10 years” and “a greater amount of FI compared with minor leakage.” Currently, the optimal cell population for transplantation, the methods, and techniques for preparing the cells, and the necessary and sufficient number of cells have not yet been fully established; however, because cell injections and transplantation have been performed safely with no reports of serious complications, it is expected that this will become an important field in the treatment of FI in the future. In summary, although no meta-analyses exist regarding anal sphincter regenerative therapy, the reviewed literature included four RCTs[ - ] and two reviews[ , ]. Thus, its level of evidence can be considered reasonably robust. VI. Treatment for Fecal Incontinence in Special Conditions A. Neurogenic and spinal cord diseases (Injuries), a more detailed description Abstract In patients with neurogenic or spinal cord diseases, stool tends to accumulate in the rectum, and it is not uncommon for the retained stool to overflow and leak. In other words, because constipation and fecal incontinence (FI) are two sides of the same coin, it is important to understand the patient's excretion cycle and guide them to go to the toilet at the right time. If spontaneous defecation is not possible, the anorectal region should be stimulated with fingers to induce defecation or the rectum should be emptied periodically by manual evacuation, suppositories, or enemas. Transanal irrigation improves the symptoms of constipation and FI as well as QoL in patients with spinal cord injury. Commentary Based on the onset mechanisms of neurogenic and spinal cord diseases, they are classified into congenital, traumatic, degenerative, ischemic, etc. Injuries to the nervous system and spinal cord often result in motor and sensory disturbances of the pelvic organs and pelvic floor, leading to difficulty in regulating bowel movements and causing constipation and FI. The frequency of FI by disease has been reported to be over 70% in patients with spinal cord injury and multiple sclerosis[ , ], over 34% in patients with spina bifida[ ], and 24% in patients with Parkinson's disease[ ]. In patients with spinal cord injury, rectal sensation is decreased or eliminated, and therefore, the urge to defecate is also decreased or eliminated. Thus, the patient will not go to the toilet if their defecation relies on the urge to defecate, and fecal impaction, in which a large amount of feces accumulates in the rectum, is likely to occur. In addition, spinal cord injury also causes characteristic defecation disorders depending on the site of injury. Injury above the conus medullaris (a caudal edge of the tapered spinal cord, usually located as high as the first lumbar vertebra) is characterized by persistent increased tone of the colonic wall and external anal sphincter, a condition called reflex bowel, leading to fecal impaction or overflow FI. In contrast, injury at the conus medullaris and cauda equina is characterized by a decrease in colonic peristalsis and persistent atonic external anal sphincter and levator ani, a condition called flaccid bowel, leading to passive FI[ ]. For patients with spinal cord injury, constipation and FI are perceived to be more serious than mobility impairment[ ], causing anxiety and resulting in a decline in QOL[ ]. However, conventional treatment is mostly empirical with little evidence[ ]. In the treatment of FI associated with neurogenic and spinal cord diseases, the following evaluations are required in addition to the usual evaluation of FI[ , ]. 1 Medical history: Patient's wishes, QoL assessment, problems with moving to the toilet, dressing and undressing, behavior of caregivers, etc. 2 Physical findings: Cognitive function, severity of spastic paralysis of the upper and lower limbs, abdominal palpation, and rectal examination, working ability of hands and fingers, walking and ambulating ability, ability to hold sitting position, motor, sensation, and reflexes of the anorectum, etc. 1. Conservative therapy a. Initial treatment 1 Fiber-rich diet and adequate fluid intake 2 Stimulation of the anorectum and use of suppositories and enemas 3 Planned defecation (timely assistance or trigger for defecation) 4 Prescription of oral medications 5 Abdominal massage 6 Manual evacuation Patients with neurogenic and spinal cord diseases tend to have stool accumulated in the rectum due to decreased activity and sensory and motor disturbances in the anorectal region. Initial treatment aims to completely empty the bowels by regularly guiding the patient to the toilet and providing defecation stimulation. The above procedures should be attempted in stages to empty the rectum in a way that is optimal for the patient. Fiber-rich diet and adequate fluid intake are the basics for improving stool consistency. Stimulation of the anorectal region by digital rectal examination or suppositories induces increased peristalsis of the left colon and defecation[ ], and a study on the timing of defecation induction in

the rectum due to decreased activity and sensory and motor disturbances in the anorectal region. Initial treatment aims to completely empty the bowels by regularly guiding the patient to the toilet and providing defecation stimulation. The above procedures should be attempted in stages to empty the rectum in a way that is optimal for the patient. Fiber-rich diet and adequate fluid intake are the basics for improving stool consistency. Stimulation of the anorectal region by digital rectal examination or suppositories induces increased peristalsis of the left colon and defecation[ ], and a study on the timing of defecation induction in patients with stroke found that inducing defecation in the morning was more effective than inducing it in the evening[ ]. Although the mechanism is unknown, it has been suggested to be related to gastro-colonic reflexes induced after breakfast. Abdominal massage has been reported to improve constipation in patients with multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injury[ , ]. Patients with fecal impaction require removal of the fecal mass by manual evacuation. In a survey of patients with spinal cord injury at home, 56% of the patients underwent manual evacuation as defecation care[ ]. For more information on care for FI in neurogenic and spinal cord diseases, please refer to IV-A-3. b. Specialized treatment 1 Transanal irrigation 2 Biofeedback therapy 3 Anal insert device 4 Tibial nerve stimulation When initial treatment is not effective, specialized treatment is indicated. The therapeutic concept for neurogenic bowel dysfunction associated with neurogenic and spinal cord diseases is illustrated in . If the treatments at the lower level are not sufficiently effective, a stepwise escalation to higher-level treatments is recommended[ , ]. Specialized treatment is indicated when initial treatment is not effective. Transanal irrigation promotes defecation by injecting lukewarm water into the rectum and left colon (see IV-B-3)[ ]. In an RCT of patients with spinal cord injury, transanal irrigation significantly improved constipation, FI, and QOL compared with conservative therapies (corresponding to initial treatment in this section)[ ]. Although there are few reports on BF therapy, it has been reported to improve FI in patients with less severe multiple sclerosis[ ]. Other specialized treatments include an anal insert device (see IV-B-4-c), and TNS (see IV-B-4-a) has been reported to have improved FI caused by incomplete spinal cord injury[ ]. 2. Surgical treatment 1 Antegrade continence enema 2 Sacral neuromodulation 3 Colostomy The improvement rate of defecation disorders caused by spinal cord injury is said to be 63% with conservative therapies[ ]; thus, surgical treatment may be an option when FI does not improve or when chronic severe constipation coexists. ACE is a treatment that involves creating an appendiceal or cecal fistula and inserting a catheter through the site to perform antegrade lavage (see IV-C-2-a). When this treatment was applied to patients with spinal cord injury, FI or constipation improved in seven of eight patients[ ]. For more information on sacral neuromodulation, please refer to IV-C-1-b and CQ5. Colostomy (see IV-C-1-c) reduced the time required for defecation care in patients with spinal cord injury and improved their QOL[ , ]. CQ5. Is sacral neuromodulation effective for the treatment of fecal incontinence caused by spinal cord injury? Statement • Sacral neuromodulation is proposed to be performed, as it may improve fecal incontinence caused by incomplete spinal cord injury. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Commentary Sacral neuromodulation is a treatment that improves defecation disorders and lower urinary tract dysfunction by electrical stimulation of the sacral nerve (see IV-C-1-b). Among 11 patients with cauda equina syndrome, 5 of the 8 patients who responded positively to test stimulation received a stimulator implant, and all experienced improvements in fecal incontinence (FI)[ ]. However, this treatment was ineffective for all three patients with complete spinal cord injury[ ]. There were reports of improvement in FI in patients with incomplete spinal cord injury and spina bifida[ - ]. In one of the reports, 29 of 36 patients were implanted with a stimulator, and FI and QoL were improved in 28 patients[ ]. Additionally, in a study involving 10 patients with incomplete paraplegia, pre-treatment control of defecation urge was limited to less than 1 minute in all cases. After treatment, some patients could control their defecation urges for up to 15 minutes, demonstrating significant improvement[ ]. The above findings are based on papers published up to 2014, evaluated in the first edition of these guidelines, but there have been very few reports since 2015 on the efficacy of this treatment for defecation disorders, including FI, caused by spinal cord injury. This lack of recent data is likely attributable to the previously reported limited efficacy for patients with spinal cord injury, which may have discouraged further studies. Nevertheless, in 2020, the efficacy of this treatment for neurogenic bowel disorder (NBD) in

some patients could control their defecation urges for up to 15 minutes, demonstrating significant improvement[ ]. The above findings are based on papers published up to 2014, evaluated in the first edition of these guidelines, but there have been very few reports since 2015 on the efficacy of this treatment for defecation disorders, including FI, caused by spinal cord injury. This lack of recent data is likely attributable to the previously reported limited efficacy for patients with spinal cord injury, which may have discouraged further studies. Nevertheless, in 2020, the efficacy of this treatment for neurogenic bowel disorder (NBD) in 41 patients with neurogenic bladder associated with defecation disorder was reported, with significant improvement in NBD scores and good long-term outcomes in 26 patients, suggesting the efficacy of this treatment for incomplete spinal cord injury[ ]. B. Dementia Abstract For fecal incontinence (FI) due to dementia, the relationship between the patient's surroundings and FI should be analyzed, the defecation environment should be improved, and the patient should be guided to defecate at appropriate times based on their bowel diary or other information. In cases of FI or stool playing, it is important to respect the patient's self-esteem and to strive to build a good relationship with the patient. Commentary The pathophysiology of FI in patients with dementia includes cognitive dysfunctional FI, in which the patient defecates in a location that is not the toilet or in an inappropriate container as a result of behavioral abnormalities, and overflow FI, in which the patient is unable to void due to a lack of the urge to defecate or impaired judgment, resulting in leakage of feces that have filled the rectum[ , , ]. Chronic FI is found in approximately 50% of patients with dementia residing in elderly care facilities[ , ]. Symptoms of dementia are broadly classified into core symptoms (memory impairment, disorientation, aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, etc.) and behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD). BPSD consists of behavioral symptoms (verbal abuse/violence, wandering, rejection, deinhibition, FI, etc.) and psychological symptoms (sense of anxiety, depression, emotional blunting, hallucination/delusion, etc.)[ ]. BPSD is a secondary disorder caused by core symptoms, and physical, environmental, and psychosocial factors are deeply involved in the emergence of these symptoms; they may be triggered by an unfamiliar and uncomfortable environment or by the relationship with the caregiver[ ]. The same is true for the triggers of FI and stool playing (mistaking stool for other objects, playing with stool in the toilet bowl, etc.), which are behavioral symptoms[ ]. The treatment for FI in patients with dementia is the same as conservative therapies for general FI, but conducting a behavioral analysis of the patient with information collected from the patient, their family, and caregivers can help identify necessary measures. In other words, the relationship between the patient's surroundings and FI should be examined (FI may occur if the patient does not know where the toilet is located). The location and circumstances in which FI occurs, the patient's reaction to FI, and the reactions of those around the patient should be observed. The discomfort felt after defecating in the diaper may cause the patient to get stool on their hands and rub it on their clothes while trying to remove the stool. Because patients with dementia often cannot express their urge to defecate and may express it as BPSD, such as wandering, a bowel diary or other records are useful for behavioral analysis[ , ]. It is also important to consider whether the caregiver's response is appropriate. If the caregiver gets angry or blames the patient with dementia for FI, the patient's self-esteem may be damaged, possibly leading to anger. In addition, behavioral symptoms, including FI, may become more severe as a form of rebellion against the caregiver's inappropriate response[ ]. Based on the results of behavioral analysis and assessment of the surrounding environment, appropriate environmental adjustments should be made for each patient. The basics include displaying signs to the toilet, guiding the patient to defecate at the timing confirmed using their bowel diary, improving the environment by adjusting lighting, and reviewing the care for dementia[ , ]. In some cases, the patient may still feel a sense of shame about unhygienic behaviors (they may hide underwear soiled by feces). Thus, preventive care that respects the patient's self-esteem is required. If the patient attempts to remove the stool from the diaper on their own or play with the stool due to discomfort caused by fecal impaction, appropriate treatment of constipation can prevent these unhygienic behaviors[ ]. In response to stool playing, the caregiver should remain calm and promptly dispose of the stool. In general, specialized treatment is not indicated for FI in patients with dementia[ ]. In contrast, caregivers are placed under great mental and physical strain and may fall into

unhygienic behaviors (they may hide underwear soiled by feces). Thus, preventive care that respects the patient's self-esteem is required. If the patient attempts to remove the stool from the diaper on their own or play with the stool due to discomfort caused by fecal impaction, appropriate treatment of constipation can prevent these unhygienic behaviors[ ]. In response to stool playing, the caregiver should remain calm and promptly dispose of the stool. In general, specialized treatment is not indicated for FI in patients with dementia[ ]. In contrast, caregivers are placed under great mental and physical strain and may fall into a state of depression. Thus, a support system should be established so that caregivers do not feel isolated[ , ]. Giving caregivers time to relax and building a good relationship with patients will lead to a reduction in behavioral symptoms. C. Frail or bedridden older adults Abstract Frail or bedridden older adults are prone to overflow fecal incontinence (FI) caused by fecal impaction. Thus, fecal impaction should be prevented by regular defecation induction and planned defecation using suppositories or enemas. For FI associated with constipation, the type and dosage of laxatives should be adjusted by considering the frequency of defecation and stool consistency. Commentary Although there are various definitions of frailty, the Cardiovascular Health Study criteria[ ] deem a person frail if he/she meets three or more of the following five items: weight loss, decreased activity, decreased muscle strength, decreased walking speed, and fatigue; pre-frail if meeting one or two items; and healthy if meeting none of the items. The prevalence of FI in nursing home residents is as high as approximately 50%, and although FI is recognized among nursing home residents, it is rarely acknowledged as a problem, and treatment and care are not always proactive[ , ]. However, even in frail or bedridden older adults, treatment is often possible with assessment and understanding of the pathophysiology[ ]. Initial treatment is the same as conservative therapies for general FI, but the patient, their family, and caregivers should be interviewed regarding the patient's condition to select a feasible treatment method and to develop a treatment plan tailored to each individual patient[ ]. A characteristic condition of frail or bedridden older adults is overflow FI due to fecal impaction[ ]. The causes of fecal impaction are diverse, including long periods of time spent lying or sitting, decreased abdominal pressure during defecation, inadequate fluid and fiber intake, metabolic diseases such as hypothyroidism and hypokalemia, use of drugs that inhibit gastrointestinal motility, and neurological diseases such as cerebral infarction and Parkinson's disease[ ]. Therefore, it is important to prevent fecal impaction by inducing regular defecation and planned defecation using suppositories or enemas. In an RCT of patients with FI in a nursing home, FI was significantly improved by fecal characteristic adjustments and regular enemas[ ]. In addition, in an RCT of frail patients, FI was significantly improved by inducing defecation and exercise 5 days a week[ ]. Bedridden older adults often need to wear diapers, but if the patient is able to communicate the urge to defecate, having the patient defecate using a toilet in bed will reduce the burden on caregivers[ ]. In contrast, excessive administration of laxatives for fear of fecal impaction can cause diarrhea and incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD)[ ]. In the case of FI associated with constipation, laxatives must be controlled by considering the frequency of defecation and stool consistency. In addition, diarrhea tends to occur in patients on enteral nutrition due to (1) administration of high-concentration enteral nutrition formulas, (2) administration rate being too fast, (3) temperature of nutrition formulas being too low, (4) bacterial proliferation, and (5) a lack of dietary fiber[ ]. Anal insert device has been reported to be useful for bedridden older adults with diarrhea[ ]. For more information on care and prevention of IAD, please refer to II-A-2-c and IV-A-3. chunks.content: Core Tip: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in the intensive care unit is a serious, life-threatening condition, requiring a multidisciplinary approach. Despite advances in prophylactic strategies and critical care protocols reducing its incidence, GI bleeding remains a major concern, particularly in patients with risk factors such as coagulopathy and renal failure. Enhanced management strategies are crucial, yet the condition is still associated with significant morbidity and mortality, especially in cases complicated by multi-organ failure. The purpose of this compilation of the most recent literature is to review the most up-to-date recommendations and protocols to be followed for the management of a patient with GI bleeding in an intensive care unit. INTRODUCTION Overview of gastrointestinal bleeding Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common and potentially life-threatening medical condition that occurs when there is bleeding from any part of the digestive tract, which includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine. The severity of the bleeding can range from mild to severe, with the latter often requiring immediate medical attention and intervention[ ]. Patients with GI bleeding (GIB) may present with a variety of symptoms, including hematemesis (vomiting of blood), melena (black, tarry stools), and hematochezia, depending on the location and severity of the bleeding[ ]. When a patient presents with GIB, prompt assessment and resuscitation are vital. The initial management includes stabilizing the patient, assessing the severity of the bleeding, and determining the source of the bleeding[ - ]. Overall, the management of GIB requires a multidisciplinary approach, involving prompt assessment, resuscitation, risk stratification, and the timely application of appropriate therapeutic interventions. Epidemiology and incidence in intensive care unit GIB is a serious clinical event that poses a significant risk to life, leading to over 400000 hospital admissions annually in the United States. This condition also places a considerable financial strain on healthcare systems[ ]. The incidence of upper GI bleed (UGIB) is estimated to be around 67 cases per 100000 individuals, whereas lower GIB (LGIB) occurs at a rate of approximately 36 cases per 100000 individuals. Notably, LGIB is more prevalent in men than in women, which can be attributed to the higher prevalence of vascular diseases and diverticulosis in the male population[ ]. Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) remains the leading cause of acute UGIB, accounting for up to 67% of all cases[ ]. The overall incidence of acute UGIB, especially cases related to PUD, showed a marked decline toward the end of the twentieth century. In recent decades, however, this trend has plateaued, with the incidence rates stabilizing in the twenty-first century within the United States[ ]. Pathophysiology of GIB GIB is a complex and multifaceted medical condition that arises from various underlying pathologies affecting the digestive tract. The normal stomach mucosa maintains a delicate balance between protective and aggressive factors, and disruption of this equilibrium can lead to the development of GI ulcers and subsequent bleeding. Aggressive factors, such as gastric acid, abnormal motility, pepsin, bile salts, use of alcohol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, as well as infection with microorganisms, can overwhelm the protective mechanisms, including mucus secretion, bicarbonate production, gastroprotective prostaglandin synthesis, and normal tissue microcirculation[ ]. The severity of macroscopic lesions developed in GIB can be assessed using a semiquantitative scale[ ]. The incidence of GIB varies with age, gender, and geographical location, and it is associated with severe complications, including hemorrhages, perforations, GI obstruction, and malignancy. Consequently, this clinical condition represents a significant health problem worldwide due to its high morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. Pharmacists practicing in critical care settings require a comprehensive understanding of the causes and consequences of bleeding, as well as the mechanisms of hemostasis, in order to provide appropriate management and treatment for patients with GIB[ , ]. The hemostatic mechanism plays a crucial role in the pathophysiology of GIB. Platelets, coagulation, and the vessel wall work in intimate cooperation to maintain hemostasis. The unique acidic environment of the stomach can have a significant impact on the various physiological stages of hemostasis, potentially contributing to the development and progression of GIB. Additionally, patients with inherited and acquired bleeding disorders, as well as those undergoing therapeutic anticoagulation, are at an increased risk for severe bleeding events[ ]. Stress ulcers are gastric lesions that occur in critically ill patients due to factors like mucosal ischemia, increased gastric acid production, and impaired protective mechanisms, often exacerbated by conditions such as hypotension, mechanical ventilation, or corticosteroid use. Steroids can worsen the risk of stress ulcers by increasing gastric acid secretion, altering electrolyte balance, and suppressing the immune system. Hypotension, resulting from shock, bleeding, or sepsis, disrupts tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery, contributing to organ dysfunction. CLASSIFICATION OF GIB UGIB UGIB are defined as bleeding along the GI tract from the mouth to the duodenum proximal to the ligament of Treitz[ ]. Common causes of UGIB include duodenal ulcer (20%-30%), gastric or duodenal erosions (20%-30%), esophageal varices (15%-20%), gastric ulcer (10%-20%), Mallory-Weiss tears (MWT, 5%-10%), erosive esophagitis (5%-10%), angioma (5%-10%), arteriovenous malformations (< 5%), GI stromal tumors (GIST), and hemobilia[ ]. As mentioned above, the most common causes of UGIB are ulcers of the stomach or duodenum, manifestations of PUD, which presents with a lifetime incidence rate between 5% and 10% in Western countries[ ]. The two most common causative agents of GI bleeds from PUD are Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection and chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use, with an estimated 90% of patients with duodenal ulcers and over 70% of patients with gastric ulcers testing positive for H. pylori infection. Alcohol and smoking of tobacco products have also both been implicated in increased risk of developing PUD[ , ]. Erosion of the stomach lining falling short of ulceration is another common cause of UGIB, with H. pylori infection and NSAID use [particularly aspirin (ASA) and other nonselective COX-inhibitors] also demonstrated to be the main causative agents[ ]. Gastroesophageal varices are another common cause of UGIB, with 80% of variceal bleeding occurring along the esophagus itself, although one study found that 27.3% of fundal varices present with active bleeding compared to 19.6% of esophageal varices[ ]. Esophageal varices are commonly a consequence of portal hypertension, the most common cause of which is cirrhosis, with ruptured esophageal varices the most common cause of mortality in patients with cirrhosis[ ]. MWT and erosive esophagitis, also known as esophageal erosion, are two other common causes of UGIB originating in the esophagus itself. MWT are longitudinal lacerations in the mucosa of the distal esophagus, are most commonly involved in episodes of vomiting following acute alcohol abuse, and present with hematemesis in 85% of cases. The bleeding is generally petechial and mild with a self-limiting course[ , ]. Erosive esophagitis is caused by breaks in the esophageal mucosa, most commonly as a consequence of gastroesophageal reflux disease[ ]. Dieulafoy lesions are rare submucosal vascular malformations that can progress to bleeding along the GI tract, occurring without any ulceration or erosion and most commonly seen along the lesser curvature of the stomach[ ]. Gastric hemangiomas are rare benign tumors that can progress to UGIB, although they more commonly cause occult bleeding. Due to the scarcity of these tumors, a definitive diagnostic approach does not exist, and they are often not biopsied in order to avoid progression of further bleeding[ - ]. GIST are rare tumors arising in the mesenchyme of the GI tract that can progress to bleeding of the stomach and present as UGIB. They occur sporadically without any apparent heritability pattern or known environmental or lifestyle risk factors, but KIT oncogene expression has been connected to increased incidence of GIST occurrence[ ]. Hemobilia is defined as bleeding from the liver and the biliary tree. Iatrogenic injury after hepatobiliary intervention or surgery is the most common cause of hemobilia, but rare cases have been documented of hemobilia secondary to accidental trauma or a neoplastic, infectious, or inflammatory process[ ]. Lower GI bleeds Lower GI bleeds are classified as bleeding along the GI tract distal to the ligament of Treitz. Common causes of lower GI bleeds include anal fissures, angiodysplasia (vascular ectasia), colonic carcinoma and colonic polyps, diverticular disease, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (ulcerative proctitis/colitis & Crohn's disease), and internal hemorrhoids[ ]. Diverticular bleeding of the large intestine is a common cause of lower GI hemorrhage, with patients generally presenting with massive but painless rectal hemorrhage. It is the most common cause of acute severe LGIB. They develop when arteries within the diverticulum of the colon erode or tear and bleed directly into the colon, and like many other lower GI bleeds, their exact pathophysiological pathways of development aren’t fully understood. Several causes have been implicated in increasing risk of diverticular bleeding common to other lower GI bleeds, such as
